title: 3D Geometry
coreInsight: Volume measures three-dimensional filling while surface area measures exposed two-dimensional boundary, and both can be built from simpler layers or faces.
targetLearnerRealization: Volume counts cubic units in layers, while surface area counts only exposed square faces; contacts hide faces without removing volume.
learningObjectives: Build prism and cylinder volume as base area times height.
Distinguish cubic volume units from square surface-area units.
Count only exposed faces after solids join.
Explain length, area, and volume scale factors k, k², and k³.
Use nets and face inventories to reason about surface area.

continuity.openingCallback: Treat a familiar 2D region as one layer, then stack congruent layers to create three-dimensional filling.
closingSeeds: Cutting exposed faces open creates a flat net that can be folded back into the same solid.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Surface area and volume are interchangeable measurements.
Internal or covered faces should be counted as exposed.
Linear scale, area scale, and volume scale use the same factor.
Square and cubic units can be used interchangeably.

beats.purpose: Separate filling from exposed boundary through a unit-cube rectangular prism.
beats.expectedRealization: A 3-by-2-by-4 prism holds 24 unit cubes, while surface area counts six rectangular outer faces.
beats.transitionIn: A 3-by-2 rectangle covers six square units. Stack four identical copies as layers and ask a new measurement question.
beats.whyNow: The shared base makes G3's area meaning the direct source of volume while keeping surface distinct.
beats.entryBridge: Count cubes layer by layer for filling; count only outer square tiles for skin.
beats.exitBridge: Four 6-cube layers give volume 24, while the six face rectangles total 52 square units.
learnerPrompts: How many unit cubes fill the prism?
Which measurement describes its exposed skin?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Volume is 24 cubic units and surface area is 52 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 3×2 cubes per layer and four layers; then separately total the six exposed rectangles.

visual.ariaLabel: A three by two by four prism compared by twenty-four cubic filling units and fifty-two exposed square units

resolution.takeaway: Volume fills with cubes; surface area covers exposed faces with squares.

beats.purpose: Show why joining solids hides two face descriptions at each contact.
beats.expectedRealization: Two unit cubes joined face-to-face have volume 2 but surface area 10, not 12.
beats.transitionIn: Bring two unit cubes together until one face from each occupies the same internal contact.
beats.prompt: Two unit cubes are glued face-to-face. What are the volume and exposed surface area of the solid?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Both cubes remain, but the two touching faces are internal.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with 12 face squares and remove one face from each cube at the contact.

steps.body: Volume adds: 1+1=2. Surface area starts at 6+6=12, then loses two exposed faces: 12−2=10.

resolution.takeaway: A contact hides two faces but removes no cubic filling.

beats.purpose: Generalize layer counting to prisms and cylinders.
beats.expectedRealization: Each unit of height adds one congruent base-area layer.
beats.transitionIn: The prism used a six-square base repeated four times. Replace the rectangular base with a circle.
beats.prompt: A cylinder has base area 25π square units and height 7 units. What is its volume?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Seven layers of area 25π give 175π cubic units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Volume is base area times perpendicular height.

resolution.takeaway: Prism and cylinder volume stack congruent base-area layers.

beats.purpose: Derive cubic volume scaling when all dimensions change.
beats.expectedRealization: A dilation by k multiplies surface area by k² and volume by k³.
beats.transitionIn: Double length, width, and height of the prism simultaneously.
beats.prompt: A solid is dilated by scale factor 2. By what factors do its surface area and volume change?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Two dimensions produce 2² on faces; three produce 2³ in filling.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count how many independent length factors appear in area and volume.

steps.body: Each face area receives two factors of 2, while each volume layer count receives three: 2²=4 and 2³=8.

resolution.takeaway: Dimension determines the power of the scale factor.

beats.purpose: Name volume and surface formulas after layer and face meanings are built.
beats.expectedRealization: Formulas are inventories of layers or exposed faces.
beats.name: Volume and surface area
beats.conciseDefinition: Volume counts cubic units filling a solid and often equals base area times height. Surface area counts square units covering only the exposed boundary faces.
beats.formalization: prism/cylinder V=Bh · rectangular prism SA=2(lw+lh+wh) · dilation: length k, area k², volume k³
beats.memoryHook: Stack the base for volume; unfold the skin for surface area.

beats.purpose: Apply exposed-face accounting to unequal cubes and a percent increase.
beats.expectedRealization: The small cube adds six face units but hides its bottom and one unit patch of the large top, netting four over the original 24.
beats.transitionIn: A unit-cube pair hid two equal faces. Attach a smaller cube to only part of a larger cube's top face.
beats.whyNow: The learner can separate volume from surface and is ready to account for a partial covered patch before calculating percent change.
beats.entryBridge: Find original surface area, add the small cube's faces, remove both contact descriptions, then compare with the original.
beats.exitBridge: Net added area 4 over original 24 is 1/6≈16.7%, closest to 17%.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A unit-cube model with exposed faces highlighted and contact faces hidden.
learnerPrompts: What is the original large cube's surface area?
Which two unit-square regions become hidden at contact?
Why is adding all six small-cube faces wrong?
What is the net new exposed area?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The surface area rises by about 17%.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The small cube's bottom and the covered 1×1 patch of the large cube are both no longer exposed.

steps.title: Account for contact
steps.body: The small cube contributes 6, but its bottom and the covered patch remove 2 exposed square units, so net change is 4.

resolution.takeaway: Surface changes depend on exposure, not simply on how many faces a new solid owns.

beats.purpose: Coordinate diameter-to-radius conversion with squared base area and linear height.
beats.expectedRealization: Swapping diameter and height is not volume-neutral because radius is squared; the volumes are 108π and 216π.
beats.transitionIn: Layer count is height, but each circular layer's area depends on radius squared. Swap the two given dimensions and see why their roles matter.
beats.whyNow: The learner can build cylinder volume from layers and can distinguish length factors that enter once from radius factors that enter twice.
beats.entryBridge: Halve each diameter, find each base area, then multiply by its own height.
beats.exitBridge: The wider can's base grows fourfold while height halves, leaving twice the volume; Alex:Felicia=1:2.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A base-area layer swept through height.
learnerPrompts: Why does swapping 6 and 12 not preserve volume?
What radius and base area does Alex's can have?
What radius and base area does Felicia's can have?
How does four times the base and half the height affect volume?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Convert diameters to radii first; only the radius is squared in πr²h.

steps.title: Alex's layers
steps.body: Radius 3 gives base 9π; height 12 gives volume 108π.

steps.title: Felicia's layers
steps.body: Radius 6 gives base 36π; height 6 gives volume 216π.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: 108π:216π=1:2. The base factor 4 and height factor 1/2 combine to factor 2.

resolution.takeaway: Dimensions with different roles cannot be swapped blindly.

beats.purpose: Assess volume and surface area together.
beats.whyNow: Return to a rectangular prism after contextual solids.
beats.entryBridge: Compute filling and skin on separate lines.
beats.exitBridge: A 5×3×2 prism has volume 30 and surface area 62.
learnerPrompts: Which calculation counts cubes and which counts face squares?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Volume is 30 and surface area is 62.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use lwh for volume and twice the sum of the three face-pair areas for surface area.

resolution.takeaway: Keep filling and boundary inventories separate.

beats.whyNow: Make unit meaning, not arithmetic, the target.
beats.entryBridge: Ask whether the measurement covers faces or fills space.
beats.exitBridge: A box capacity uses cubic centimeters.
learnerPrompts: What does one counted unit look like?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Volume is measured in cubic centimeters.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Capacity fills three-dimensional space, so its unit is a cube.

steps.body: A 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box holds 24 one-centimeter cubes: 24 cm³.

resolution.takeaway: Square units cover surfaces; cubic units fill solids.

beats.purpose: Assess exposed-face correction over multiple contacts.
beats.entryBridge: Start with all cube faces and remove two per join.
beats.exitBridge: Four cubes in a straight chain have three joins and 18 exposed faces.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Four cubes own 24 faces; three contacts hide two face descriptions each.

beats.whyNow: Use a non-double factor and compare area with volume.
beats.entryBridge: Raise the length factor to the measurement dimension.
beats.exitBridge: Factor 3 makes surface area ×9 and volume ×27.
learnerPrompts: How many independent length directions does each measure use?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Surface area grows by 9 and volume by 27.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 3² for area and 3³ for volume.

beats.purpose: Assess exposed-face inventory when one face is intentionally absent.
beats.whyNow: Finish with a surface that is not a closed six-face box.
beats.entryBridge: List only material faces; the top opening contributes no area.
beats.exitBridge: Base 24 plus side rectangles 24 and 16 totals 64.
learnerPrompts: Which rectangle would a closed-box formula wrongly include?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The open box uses 64 square units of material.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count one 6×4 base, two 6×2 sides, and two 4×2 sides—no top.

resolution.takeaway: Surface area counts the faces that actually exist and are exposed.

beats.purpose: Consolidate layers, exposure, units, and dimensional scaling.
beats.expectedRealization: The target measurement determines the inventory and exponent.
beats.transitionIn: Prisms, cylinders, cube contacts, and open boxes all became manageable once filling and skin were counted separately.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable 3D measurement routine? Select all four.

options.text: Decide whether the target is filling or exposed boundary.
For volume, multiply base area by layer height.
For surface area, count only existing exposed faces.
Use square units and k² for area; cubic units and k³ for volume.

response.feedback: Each action protects one dimension of the model.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Name the target, build its inventory, and carry the correct dimension.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four prevent face, contact, and unit mix-ups.

steps.body: Volume adds material layers even when hidden inside; surface area ignores internal contacts and counts only the outer skin.

resolution.takeaway: Fill with cubes; cover with squares; hide contacts.

beats.purpose: Create the approved transition to flat nets and spatial visualization.
beats.expectedRealization: A solid's exposed face inventory can be cut and unfolded without changing face shapes or adjacency along uncut edges.
beats.transitionIn: Surface area counted an outer skin made of flat faces. Imagine cutting some edges and laying that skin on a table.
beats.prompt: What must a flat arrangement of faces preserve so it can fold back into the same solid without overlap?
beats.takeaway: A valid net keeps face shapes and enough shared-edge relationships to reconstruct the solid.

notes: Design: a rectangular base is stacked into cube layers to distinguish volume from exposed face area. Cube contacts hide two face descriptions without removing volume, cylinders generalize base-area layers, and dimensional scaling separates k² from k³. Authentic problems apply partial contact and swapped cylinder dimensions.

Beat outline: layers-versus-skin anchor -> touching faces -> base-area layers -> dimensional scaling -> name -> authentic cube surface -> authentic cylinder transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> net hook.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full timelines. Existing generic choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.

Generated results were verified through cube-layer counts, face-pair inventories, contact corrections, and dimensional scaling, with independent net or direct-product audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
